chapter_theme: The opening of Pattinathar's antadhi on Ekambar of Kanchi, a Thirumurai text and not a cipher poem. The first nine verses are a devotee's address: a confession of false service, the Lord's form and feet, the worth of the devotees' company, and a refusal to sing any other god. From 863 the poem turns into kovai-style love poetry set on Ekambar's Kailasa: the hero sees the hill girl in the millet field, comes with the pretext of a lost elephant or a hunt, and the girl and her friend speak of fear, gossip and parting.
structure_note: An antadhi: each verse opens with the sound that closes the one before (854 தொண்டனென்பணிகொள்ளுதியோ கச்சியேகம்பனே, 855 ஏகம்பனே; 878 எய்தியதே, 879 இயங்கும்). Every verse names Ekambar or Kambar of Kachi, and from 863 his Kailasa is the mountain of the love poems. 854 to 862 are bhakti; 863 to 878 follow the kovai sequence of the kurinji field: first sight (863), the hero's pretexts (864, 866, 869), the friend and the girl on fear and gossip (871, 876), and the parrots and the field at the end of the season (877, 878). The speakers are not marked and are supplied from the kovai convention.

854.reading: The poet confesses he does not know the path the true servants walk, has never done good service among the hand-servants, speaks a false service and praises the Lord only outwardly, to eat; and asks whether Ekambar of Kachi will take even this servant's service.
854.nuance: பொய்த்தொண்டு and புறம்புறமே (outwardly, outwardly) are the poet's charge against himself; the verse does not ask forgiveness but whether the Lord will accept the false service as it is. Pattinathar's legend of the renounced merchant is not in the verse.

855.reading: The poet calls Ekambar the one who rules him, the Lord who pities the gods and gives them enjoyment for many days, who wears the swelling five-mouthed serpent shining like a gold necklace, wears the fine ash, and is like a great golden mountain to the one who cherishes him.
855.nuance: The verse is an address and not a request. ஐவாய் நாகம், the five-mouthed serpent worn as an ornament, and the ash on a golden body set the Lord's form that 888 to 898 will describe limb by limb.

856.reading: The poet says he has fixed the Lord's shining name in his mind, has scraped away his hard karma, laughed at the poverty of those who do not serve Ekambar of Kachi with its bee-humming groves, and become clear enough to wear the feet of the Lord's devotees.
856.nuance: ஏழைமை, wretchedness or poverty, is what the poet sees in those who do not serve; the laugh is scorn and not pity. The feet he wears (அடியார் அடி பூண) are the devotees', not the Lord's, a step down the Saiva hierarchy that the Tirumanthiram also honours.

857.reading: The poet says his mind has gone and grown clear at the Lord's holy form, that there is no more doubt of the gracious hand that gives, and that he has gained the state of having the dust of the feet of those who rejoice in Ekambar, whose body shines like the red evening sky, set on his head.
857.nuance: தளிதரு தூளி, the dust the temple gives or the dust of the feet of those at the temple, is loose; the plain sense is that the devotees' foot-dust on his head is the gain. ஐயம் இனி இலை (no more doubt) is the hinge: clarity, not merit, is what the form gives.

858.reading: The poet says he gained and rejoiced, learned and rejoiced in the Lord's growing fame so as to offer archana always and sweeten his thought, and calls on Ekambar, who delights in the hold of Kachi and comes on the bull with the hooded serpent wound as his belt, naming his twin feet.
858.nuance: The verse plays கச்சி (Kanchi) against கச்சு (belt): the serpent is the belt the Lord of Kachi wears. அர்ச்சனை marks this as temple devotion, which the later Siddhar poets in this corpus mock; Pattinathar here is a Thirumurai devotee.

859.reading: The ground where the Lord's feet stood was beyond the reach of Vishnu, and the crown where his head stood became hard for the lotus-born Brahma to see; the poet asks how we are to worship the trident-bearing Ekambar whose bull roars like thunder in dark clouds.
859.nuance: The myth is the pillar of fire whose foot and crown Vishnu and Brahma could not find. The question யாம் எங்ஙனே வணங்குவதே is not refusal: if the gods could not reach his limits, the human worshipper's bowing is beyond its object, and that is offered as praise.

860.reading: The poet says that bowing is for the Lord's feet, that we know no fellowship but that of those infatuated enough to bow, and that apart from singing cool Kachi Ekambam of the one who bent the mountain into a bow with the strong serpent as string, the poetic excellence that sings another god does not count.
860.nuance: கணக்கன்று, 'it is no account', makes the claim about poetry and not about the gods: verse spent on another god is wasted craft. மையல், infatuation, is used of devotion without irony, the word the love verses will use of desire.

861.reading: The poet tells the good people to listen to one thing for their good: seeing Kachi Ekambam of Haran mixed with love, stand and worship him with the words that he set the fiery discus to cut down Jalandhara and that he made all of Daksha's sacrifice ... permanent.
861.nuance: நிரந்தரமாகச் செய்தாய் of Daksha's sacrifice is odd, since the myth has the Lord wreck it; it may mean he made it endless by stopping it, or be ironic, or carry a sense of நிரந்தரம் I cannot fix. The frame, a devotee instructing others how to praise, is clear.

862.reading: Some called his locks lightning, his throat a cloud, his body's colour gold; those who have worn his golden feet, whatever they say of his appearing, do not know parting from him; and the natures by which all the worlds hold their place are said to be those of Kachi Ekambar.
862.nuance: வெளிப்பாடு, manifestation, is what the comparisons describe; the verse sets the devotees' not-parting (பிரிந்தறியார்) above any description of the form, and then makes the Lord the ground on which the worlds stand.

863.reading: On the rich Kailasa of walled Kachi Ekambar, whom the gods and the unfailing ascetics worship, the grace of a golden peacock, red-streaked eyes, curled hair and a waist that bends in softness have brought love to birth.
863.nuance: The love poem begins here without notice: the subject of காதல் விளைத்தன is the hill girl's body, and the speaker is the hero at first sight, by the kovai convention. The peacock and the striped eyes are the stock comparisons of that moment.

864.reading: The friend tells the girl, their flower-creeper, that a youth like Murugan, asking after an elephant that has not left off its rage, does not leave the millet field while it is day, on the heavenly Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar whose devotees bear the mark of the Lady's embrace.
864.nuance: Asking after a lost elephant is the hero's pretext for staying near the girl, a fixed motif of the kurinji field (வேழம் வினாதல்). The friend's noticing that he will not leave is itself the sign (குறிப்பு) that she has read him. The first two lines, on devotees who bear the scar of embracing Uma, are the shrine-praise frame and strain the syntax.

865.reading: On the kongu-crested Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar with its flowering groves, a speaker addresses the golden one who is like a goddess, and says something about seeing and pained feet if she came playing in the spreading stone waterfall.
865.nuance: கண்டு அடி வருத்தே at the close does not resolve: either the hero fears her feet would be hurt on the rocks, or someone saw her and was wounded by the sight. பாங்கு ஒத்திருந்தனையார் (one fit to be a companion) suggests the hero asking the friend's help; I can't fix the speaker.

866.reading: The girl or her friend says that the youth has a body that gives pain, a leaf-gift in his hand and questions about a strong beast, and that apart from searching and standing there, the only work for us on the Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar, who grants correction, is guarding the millet field.
866.nuance: தழை in the hand is the leaf-garment the hero offers as a gift (தழை ஈதல்), and வன்மா வினவும் his pretext of a lost animal; the speaker sets his business against theirs, which is only the field. The editor's note glosses துரு as searching (ஆராய்ச்சி), which gives துருத்து அந்து as 'searching and ending', a reading the line barely supports.

867.reading: The friend asks whether the youth who left his deer and came into this field, with his elephant, has come to steal our thought and our gaze, and asks the great ones, with the Mother and those flower eyes, to grant grace, on the lovely Kailasa of Kambar who takes us and our service as his.
867.nuance: கவர்வ என்றோ (is it to steal?) is the friend's guess at the youth's motive. Who the பெரியீர் are who should grant grace, the hero addressed in the plural or the Lady and her flower eyes, is unclear; the request may be the friend's hint that the hero should act.

868.reading: The girl says that the bowman who went off after the deer with his arrow, urging on the elephant in the darkness of the slope, has by the flicker of his eyelid left her bewildered, and asks whether there is any lord for us in this world, on the golden Kailasa of Kambar who gives grace.
868.nuance: மருளைத் தரு (that gives bewilderment) and எங்கோ இலை உண்டு (is there a king for us?) are the two clear phrases; the middle, with the deer, the arrow and the elephant in the dark, is a hunt scene whose grammar I can't settle. The 'king' is the hero as the girl's only protector, by convention.

869.reading: The friend says that in the field on Ingoy hill of Ekambar with the sharp axe, all the hunting of deer, boar and elephant that the youth follows is false, since what is in his mind is our flower-creeper, whose breasts he has not won, and that the serpent-waisted one has come at the scent.
869.nuance: பொய்யானவை, 'those are false', names the hunt as the hero's pretext outright, the convention stated rather than hinted. ஈங்கோய்மலை is a separate Saiva hill shrine, named here for Ekambar; the last line, with the hooded serpent's waist and the scent (பரிமணம்), is loose.

870.reading: In the field on the flower Kailasa of Kambar with the three-headed spear, where rutting elephants whose brows shed great pearls and thunder-voiced lions roam, the hero says that because of his desire for the girl whose laugh is like pearls, not approaching the hill has become hard.
870.nuance: வெற்பு அசார்வு அரிதே reads best as 'staying away from the hill is hard', the hero drawn past the dangers the first lines heap up; it could also be 'reaching the hill is hard', the dangers winning. The pearls from the elephant's brow and the pearls of her teeth are the verse's one image, twice.

871.reading: The friend or girl tells the mountain lord that this is not the Kailasa ruined by the lion's night, and that what stays hard here for us is that we fear our elders; the frame praises Kambar, who gave an eye's grace to the one who offered his own eye when his thousand flowers fell short.
871.nuance: The first two lines tell the story of Vishnu offering his lotus eye as the thousandth flower; the third, with அரி (lion, or Vishnu) and கங்குல் (night), is dark to me. The clear close, எம் ஐயர்க்கு அஞ்சுதும், is the kovai moment when the girl's side pleads fear of her kinsmen to the hero.

872.reading: On the long Kailasa of Kachi Ekambar, who opened his fiery eye so that the five-arrowed Kama fell to ash and who delights to dwell low in loving hearts, the speaker tells of an elephant falling down the slope so that your tusk survives, and asks whether this wide drum is yours or not.
872.nuance: The last two lines, with குஞ்சரம், கொம்பு, கும்பம், a variant மூழ்கும் and the drum (முரசு), do not yield a reading I trust; it may be the hero's hunting fame or the public noise of the affair. The burning of Kama in the first line, in a verse of love, is the poem's standing irony.

873.reading: In the dim darkness on the Kailasa of Uma's husband, lord of Thiruvekambam, who gave the son and guards lives as mother and father, the bamboo-shouldered girl is with our swing when a spotted beast leaps at the fragrant vengai and a clash breaks out.
873.nuance: வேங்கை is both the tree and the tiger, and பகடு is bull, buffalo or elephant; the scene is a fight between animals by the swing in the dark, or a tiger's attack, and either reading leaves the point unclear. The frame, the Lord as mother and father of lives (தாய் தந்தையாய் உயிர் காப்போன்), is the verse's plain claim.

874.reading: A speaker tells the golden ones that if they come they will gain a marriage, and describes the one who roams the slope of the spotted hill on Ekambar's Kailasa, giving honey, plucking flowers and driving off the parrots that feed on the cool millet.
874.nuance: The hero at the parrots and the millet is a kovai scene (he helps guard the field to be near the girl); who promises the marriage, and to whom, is not fixed by the verse. வந்தும் மணம் பெறில் can be the friend's reassurance to the girl or the hero's own hope.

875.reading: On the Kailasa of Ekambar who shot the moving cities, where hill-hunters set out pearls in season, we whose lot it is reached the curling one first; the speaker tells someone to hurry, part, and say there in what way we gained the shining pearl-water.
875.nuance: முத்தின் நீர் (pearl-water) and சுருள் முதலானும் (the curling one, perhaps the curly-haired girl) are the clues; the verse seems to send a message between the field and the hero, but the lines do not join into one sense I can defend.

876.reading: The friend says that madmen everywhere ask whether she is a goddess adorned, that the way the bow-armed hill lord parts from her makes gossip spread, and that the shameless noble vengai of the slope is named for you, on the golden Kailasa of Ekambar who smears his beauty with holy ash.
876.nuance: அலர, gossip rising, is the kovai stage after the secret meetings; the friend turns it on the hero as a reason for marriage. The variant நுமக்கே for நும்மையே changes the close from 'named after you' to 'for you'. Ash as the Lord's adornment (பூசுகையார் திருநீற்று எழில்) is the verse's shrine-frame.

877.reading: The girl asks the parrots, who have gained the right to stay in the field, to give leave for the hill lord who dwells without pity and for his servant, since her mind, troubled by the sorrow of parting, has run here and gone worshipping after him, on the crescent-touched Kailasa of unshifting Ekambar.
877.nuance: The field is harvested and the girl must leave it; the parrots that stay are her envy. அடியற்கும் விடை தமின், 'give leave also to his slave', makes her the hero's servant, the devotional word அடி turned to love. The mind that runs and worships (தொழுது சென்ற) is her own.

878.reading: The speaker asks whether the creeper has reached the cool millet field that gives joy together with the dark-eyed girl, told to make us grieve, on the thick Kailasa of Ekambar with the threefold holy eye, whom we worship as the one who makes us cross the sea of birth.
878.nuance: வல்லி எய்தியதே can be the creeper reaching the field or the girl (as creeper) arriving; and the one 'told to make us grieve' is either the field or the girl. The variant தம்மைப் பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர் தாம் turns 'us' to 'themselves'. The first line is the only doctrinal claim in the love verses: the Lord crosses one over the sea of births.

links.note: The Kural condemns those who, unrenounced in heart, live by deceiving as though renounced; Pattinathar confesses to exactly that false outward service and asks whether the Lord will take it anyway. The confession turns the Kural's verdict into a plea, and it leaves the verdict standing.

Both wear feet as an ornament (பூண்): Tirumular's devotees wear the holy feet of the great one and have no deeds left; Pattinathar's clarity is to wear the feet of the Lord's devotees. The ornament is the same, but Pattinathar steps one rank lower, to the servants' feet.

The first sight of the woman in both: the Kural's man cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a rare peahen or human; Pattinathar's hero sees the grace of a golden peacock and red-streaked eyes and love is born. Pattinathar states the effect (காதல் விளைத்தன) where the Kural leaves the man reeling.

The millet field as the place of wooing: Arunagirinathar's Murugan speaks his desire to the parrot of the millet field; Pattinathar's youth 'like Murugan' (சேயனையார்) will not leave the field by day. Pattinathar's comparison names the myth the Thiruppugazh tells.

Gossip as a gift to the lovers: the Kural's man says the town made him a present of gossip; Pattinathar's friend tells the hill lord that his partings spread the gossip (அலர) and that the field's vengai now bears his name. In both the rumour is turned toward the match rather than against it.

The woman's heart runs ahead of her to the absent man: the Kural's woman's heart climbs as she thinks of his return; Pattinathar's girl says her mind has run here and gone worshipping after the pitiless hill lord. Pattinathar adds the devotional verb தொழுது.

The same figure with the same claim: those who reach the Lord's feet swim the sea of births; Pattinathar's Ekambar is the one who makes us cross the sea of birth (பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர்). The Kural names no god; Pattinathar names Ekambar of Kachi.

source_issues: The work is Pattinathar's Thiruvekambamudaiyar Thiruvandhadhi of the eleventh Thirumurai; its first 25 verses here carry no section headings, and the speakers of the love verses (863 to 878) are not marked.
866 is printed with a terminal full stop and a variant note glossing துரு as ஆராய்ச்சி; the gloss is an editor's and does not settle the line.
872 line 3 has a space inside கும்ப முழ, apparently one word, and the variant மூழ்கும் suggests the word is corrupt.
878 has a variant note தம்மைப் பிறவிக்கடல் கடப்பிப்பவர்தாம் for the first line's நம்மை ... நாம்.
